target: AG1's argument that AI can improve everyday life, health, education, accessibility for disabled people, and workplace safety, therefore AI is good for society.
objection: AI harms economic well-being, undermines critical thinking, increases racial bias, and creates privacy risks, so these negative effects outweigh the benefits AG1 cited.

target: AG2's claim that AI inevitably increases privacy misuse and discrimination, weakens critical thinking, and harms economic stability.
objection: Those harms are not inevitable: AI can be deployed with privacy protections and bias mitigation, can be used as an educational coaching tool that strengthens thinking, and can be paired with reskilling and job-transition support to protect workers.

target: AG2's broader claim that AI harms workers, students, minorities, and privacy by default.
objection: AI can augment workers instead of replacing them, reduce cognitive load while supporting deeper reasoning, make outcomes more consistent and less racially biased, and protect privacy through on-device or privacy-preserving processing.

target: AG2's framing that AI is bad because it focuses on negative-risk dimensions while ignoring other societal goods.
objection: A judgment about whether AI is good for society must also consider benefits in health, quality of life, workplace safety, and accessibility for disabled people, not just risks like privacy, bias, and critical-thinking decline.

target: AG2's claim that AI worsens economic well-being and therefore reduces societal welfare.
objection: Productivity gains from AI can expand output and create complementary human work opportunities, so AI can improve workers' economic prospects rather than reduce them.

target: AG2's claim that AI undermines critical thinking and workplace safety.
objection: AI can be used as a Socratic learning tool that prompts justification, evidence checking, and critique, and it can also detect or predict hazards to improve workplace safety.

target: AG2's claim that AI undermines education, professional competence, and living standards.
objection: AI can improve education and professional competence, and it can raise living standards and day-to-day quality of life rather than undermining critical thinking.

target: AG2's claim that AI does not improve central determinants of societal well-being.
objection: AI can improve health and standard of living, and those are central parts of societal well-being, so AI can be good for society overall.

target: AG1's claim that AI improves health and living standards enough to support a pro-AI conclusion.
objection: AI is actually worsening living standards and health-related well-being for many people through economic harms, privacy/autonomy harms, and racial discrimination, so it does not improve societal well-being overall.

target: AG1's claim that AI deployments can be made safe enough through privacy protections, bias mitigation, and reskilling.
objection: In practice, AI is usually driven by profit and performance incentives that encourage extensive data collection, underprovide oversight, reproduce bias from historical data, and weaken critical thinking and economic stability.

target: AG2's claim that opaque AI systems prevent effective verification of privacy and fairness safeguards.
objection: AI can be deployed with privacy protections, bias mitigation, and interactive educational uses that prompt justification and evidence-checking, so opacity does not make harms inevitable.

target: AG1's assumption that privacy and fairness safeguards can be effectively verified in real deployments.
objection: Many AI systems are proprietary and opaque, with limited disclosure of model internals, training data, and decision logic, so affected users and outsiders often cannot verify that privacy or fairness protections actually work.

target: AG1's claim that privacy-by-design measures like data minimization and encryption eliminate privacy harms.
objection: AI can infer sensitive traits from non-sensitive data through statistical correlations, so reducing or encrypting raw data does not guarantee that privacy risks disappear.

target: AG2's claim that AI necessarily still creates privacy/autonomy harms despite privacy-by-design.
objection: Privacy-by-design can go beyond raw-data reduction by using differential privacy, federated or limited-data processing, strict access controls, purpose limitation, and adversarial training, which can reduce sensitive-inference and re-identification risks to sufficiently low levels.

target: AG1's claim that reducing inference and re-identification risk is enough to eliminate privacy/autonomy harms.
objection: AI can still undermine autonomy through profiling-driven behavioral steering and personalization even when sensitive re-identification is low, because people can be nudged and constrained by the system’s outputs.

target: AG1's claim that privacy safeguards will keep harmful privacy risks low in ordinary deployments.
objection: Typical AI deployments are driven by profit and performance incentives, so extensive data collection and underprovided safeguards make it unlikely that inference and re-identification risks are reduced to sufficiently low levels.

target: AG1's claim that privacy-focused safeguards also prevent racial bias and critical-thinking harms.
objection: Privacy safeguards aimed at inference and re-identification do not automatically prevent racial bias in outputs or stop educational/work uses from encouraging passive acceptance instead of independent justification.

target: AG1's claim that reducing technical privacy risks is enough to preserve autonomy.
objection: Technical privacy measures like differential privacy or federated processing do not automatically give users meaningful, revocable control over data collection or automated decisions, so autonomy harms can persist even when inference risk is low.

target: AG1's claim that differential-privacy style safeguards can keep risks sufficiently low in practice.
objection: Differential privacy depends on properly tracking cumulative privacy loss across updates and queries, and typical deployments may fail to cap that accumulation, causing effective privacy risk to rise above the safe threshold.
